rationale: A wins because it keeps the set tighter and separates the real stories cleanly: "Airbnb wants the corporate travel budget, and it's routing the expenses through Concur and Ramp" is the strongest commercial-pressure angle in the pile. B has a useful spend-management lens, but "Airbnb builds a business-travel product on top of hosts, not hotels" bleeds into "Airbnb is asking hosts to run something closer to a hotel," so the set starts paying rent twice for the same room. Both are good; A wastes less oxygen.
gaps_in_A: "off a small base it won't size" overstates the fact block. We know the base is missing; we do not know Airbnb refused to provide it.
It misses a clean standalone fintech/spend-management beat around Ramp and Concur, instead folding that audience into the corporate-travel channel angle.
"24hr" decay on the data angle is a little rigid; if Airbnb supplies denominator/methodology, that story could live longer than launch day.
gaps_in_B: "Airbnb builds a business-travel product on top of hosts, not hotels" and "Airbnb is asking hosts to run something closer to a hotel" are too close. Different addressees, same hotelization engine.
"a supply base it does not own or control" is true-looking, but it is not in the supplied update. The judge asked for grounding, not Airbnb lore.
"expense platforms is becoming the distribution channel for anything a company buys on the road" ladders too far from two named integrations. That's a trend thesis wearing one launch as a coat.
"24-hour check-in support is a staffing cost, not an amenity" asserts the burden before the facts establish who provides or pays for that support.
